questions.question: Which of the following is a fundamental physical quantity?
questions.explanation: A fundamental (base) quantity cannot be derived from other quantities. The seven SI base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity. Mass is one of them. Area, force, and velocity are derived quantities.

questions.question: Which set contains only the seven fundamental quantities in SI?
options: Mass, weight, time, temperature, voltage, mole, candela
Length, area, time, temperature, current, mole, candela
Mass, length, time, temperature, current, mole, candela
Mass, length, velocity, temperature, charge, mole, candela
questions.explanation: The seven SI base quantities are: mass, length, time, thermodynamic temperature, electric current, amount of substance (mole), and luminous intensity (candela). Option C lists exactly these (with 'current' meaning electric current).

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a derived physical quantity?
questions.explanation: A derived quantity is formed by combining base quantities. Density = mass/volume = [M L−3], so it is derived. Time, length, and current are base quantities.

questions.question: What distinguishes a base unit from a derived unit?
options: Base units are always larger in magnitude than derived units.
Base units are fundamental and independent.
Derived units are only used in chemistry, not physics.
Base units are defined solely by the mass of an object.
questions.explanation: Base units are defined independently for the fundamental quantities. Derived units are formed by combining base units (e.g., newton = kg·m/s²).

questions.question: The SI base unit for the amount of a substance is the:
questions.explanation: The SI base unit for amount of substance is the mole (mol). Kelvin is temperature, candela is luminous intensity, ampere is electric current.

questions.question: The fundamental physical quantity measured in Kelvin is:
questions.explanation: The kelvin (K) is the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature.

questions.question: The SI base unit for electric current is the:
questions.explanation: The SI base unit for electric current is the ampere (A). Volt is potential difference, ohm is resistance, coulomb is charge.

questions.question: The SI base unit for luminous intensity is the:
questions.explanation: The SI base unit for luminous intensity is the candela (cd). Lumen and lux are derived photometric units.

questions.question: Why is the kilogram considered a base unit rather than a derived unit?
options: It is the only unit that uses a prefix.
It can be broken down into grams.
It measures the amount of matter.
questions.explanation: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass, which is a fundamental quantity. The prefix 'kilo' is part of the unit name historically, but mass itself is a base quantity.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a base unit in the SI system?
questions.explanation: The newton (N) is a derived unit of force (kg·m/s²). Mole, kelvin, and candela are base units.

questions.question: The \dimensions\ of a physical quantity refer to:
options: The physical size of the object being measured.
The system of units being used.
questions.explanation: Dimensions describe a quantity in terms of the powers of fundamental quantities (M, L, T, etc.). For example, velocity has dimensions [L T−1].

questions.question: How are dimensions conventionally represented in physics?
questions.explanation: Dimensions are written inside square brackets, e.g., [M L T−2] for force.

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for Area?
questions.explanation: Area = length × length, so its dimension is [L2].

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for Velocity?
questions.explanation: Velocity = displacement / time = L / T, so [L T−1].

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for Force?
questions.explanation: Force = mass × acceleration = M × L T−2 = [M L T−2].

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for Energy?
questions.explanation: Energy = force × distance = [M L T−2] × [L] = [M L2 T−2].

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for Pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure = force / area = [M L T−2] / [L2] = [M L−1 T−2].

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for Angular Velocity?
questions.explanation: Angular velocity = angle / time. Angle is dimensionless, so dimensions = [T−1].

questions.question: A physical quantity is said to be \dimensionless\ when:
questions.explanation: A quantity is dimensionless when all its fundamental dimensions cancel out, i.e., the exponents of M, L, T are zero. It may still have a unit (e.g., radian).

questions.question: Which of the following pairs are both examples of dimensionless quantities?
questions.explanation: Strain = extension / original length (L/L = 1) and angle (arc length / radius) are both dimensionless. The other pairs are not both dimensionless.

questions.question: What does the principle of dimensional homogeneity state?
options: All terms in an equation must be exactly zero.
Dimensions on both sides must be equal.
An equation can only contain one variable.
All terms in an equation are dimensionless.
questions.explanation: The principle of dimensional homogeneity states that for a physically correct equation, the dimensions of every term on the left-hand side must equal the dimensions of every term on the right-hand side.

questions.question: Dimensional analysis can be used to:
questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis is used to check the consistency of physical equations and to derive relationships between quantities, but it cannot determine dimensionless constants.

questions.question: A major limitation of dimensional analysis is:
options: It only works for fundamental quantities.
questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis cannot determine dimensionless constants (e.g., 2π, ½) that appear in equations. It only gives the form of the relationship.

questions.question: Why can't you add quantities with different dimensions?
options: It violates the SI system rules.
questions.explanation: Adding quantities with different dimensions (e.g., length + time) is physically meaningless because they represent different kinds of quantities.

questions.question: Which has the same dimensions as Work?
questions.explanation: Work has dimensions [M L2 T−2]. Torque = force × distance = [M L T−2] × [L] = [M L2 T−2], so they have the same dimensions.

questions.question: Which has the same dimensions as Momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum p = mv = [M L T−1]. Impulse = force × time = [M L T−2] × [T] = [M L T−1]. So they are dimensionally identical.

questions.question: The MKS system stands for:
questions.explanation: MKS stands for Metre–Kilogram–Second, a coherent system of units based on these three base units.

questions.question: The unit \Newton\ is a:
questions.explanation: The newton is a derived unit of force: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². It is not a base unit.

questions.question: What do SI prefixes like \kilo\ and \milli\ represent?
questions.explanation: SI prefixes indicate multiples and submultiples of units: kilo = 103, milli = 10−3, etc.

questions.question: What is the conceptual difference between mass and weight in terms of units?
options: Mass is in kg, weight is in Newtons.
Mass is in Newtons, weight is in kg.
questions.explanation: Mass is a base quantity measured in kilograms (kg). Weight is a force (gravitational force on mass) measured in newtons (N).
